1:
The psalm has no title, and where it begins is not certain. Adam Clarke reports that in eight of Kennicott’s manuscripts it is written as part of the psalm before it, that in one it begins with the second verse, and that very likely the last verse of the preceding psalm was formerly the first verse of this — the want of a title having made the separation easy. Keil and Delitzsch observe the same join from the other side: the anonymous congregational song begins just as the Davidic poem before it closes. They read it as owing its composition to some deliverance of the nation from heathen oppression accomplished without war, deny any trace of dependence on earlier models that would compel a late date such as Hitzig’s, and set out the structure — two six-line frames enclosing eight quatrains of praise. John Calvin declines the question of authorship in five words, David or whoever was the author, and takes the argument of the psalm to be founded on the general providence by which God sustains and governs the whole world.

Why praise is comely for the upright, and for them only, occupies the rest. John Calvin says believers alone are capable of proclaiming the glory of God, since unbelievers who have never tasted his goodness cannot praise him from the heart; he reports that many read the clause as meaning that if the ungodly attempt it they profane the name rather than praise it, but holds the real sense to be that there is no exercise in which the righteous can be better employed. C.H. Spurgeon puts the same judgment in an image: praise from unpardoned professional singers is like a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout, and crooked hearts make crooked music. Keil and Delitzsch call it at once their duty and their honour. Matthew Henry notes that the psalm begins where the one before ended, since all religious exercise should both begin and end with a holy triumph in God. Augustine of Hippo warns them to rejoice not in themselves, which is not safe, but in the Lord.

The instruments are identified variously. Charles Ellicott takes the first for a trigon or three-cornered harp such as may be seen in Egyptian bas-reliefs, its number of strings uncertain because the accounts differ, and would render the second phrase as one thing, the ten-stringed psaltery, evidently more elaborate and of greater capacity; from its Greek name comes the title of the book itself, and by derivation the word meant an instrument played with the fingers, a usage he traces into old English with a line of Chaucer’s naming harps, pipes, lutes and sautry. Adam Clarke agrees that the two words should be joined rather than made into a third instrument, though he reports Calmet taking the first for the ancient lyre of three strings. John Wesley notes only that these were used in the public worship of the tabernacle, and C.H. Spurgeon that Israel was at school and used childish things to learn with. Augustine of Hippo hears the ten strings as the commandments, three and seven, and the players as men presenting their bodies a living sacrifice. On the command to play skilfully Adam Clarke turns critic: let the style of the music suit the words — a skill possessed by few singers, who can make a loud noise but cannot adapt sound to sense. John Gill and Charles Ellicott take the new song for one newly composed on recent mercies, Gill making it continual since the mercies of God are new every morning, and Ellicott finding in the phrase the mark of the revival of national psalmody after the captivity.
4:
Charles Ellicott traces the movement of thought: praise begins from the righteousness of the God of the covenant, but the phrase the word of the Lord carries the poet from its truth to its power, and so into praise of the creative act. John Gill divides the word into law and Gospel, the one just in condemning and acquitting, the other making men right when it works effectually in them. Adam Clarke grounds it in the divine wisdom, which can make no mistakes, so that promises and threatenings alike are true and the dispensations of providence equally so. C.H. Spurgeon says God writes with a pen that never blots, speaks with a tongue that never slips and acts with a hand that never fails,. On the earth being full of his goodness Adam Clarke answers the complainers: to hear its worthless inhabitants, one would think God dispensed evil and not good, whereas everything his hand touches is marked with mercy.

What the word was that made the heavens is answered differently. John Gill makes it the essential Word, the interpreter of his Father’s mind, who spoke on the six days of creation. C.H. Spurgeon goes further and finds all three persons of the Godhead in the verse, since the word rendered breath is elsewhere rendered Spirit, so that the three persons unite in creating; and he adds that it is easier for God to make the universe than for a man to breathe, since man borrows the breath in his nostrils from his Maker. Charles Ellicott flattens the second clause: the breath of his mouth is plainly only a synonym for word. Keil and Delitzsch take the same view with a reason, that the breath is the material of which the word is formed and its bearer, so that the phrase means the operation of his commanding omnipotence. John Wesley keeps to the wonder: God made this admirable structure and all its glorious stars not with great pains and time but with one single word.

The heap of waters divides the entry. Charles Ellicott says the image explains itself, as we speak of waves mountains high, without reference to the crossing of the Red Sea or the Jordan, and still less to heaps of corn, since the storehouses of the next clause are reservoirs; but he records that the Greek, the Latin and all the ancient interpreters read a different word, a skin, and refer the whole to rain, the clouds being considered as bottles. Keil and Delitzsch keep the heap and press the harvest sense of the word, the waters of the sea being firmly held together and rising above the level of the continents. John Gill dates the piling to the third day of creation. Adam Clarke turns the same thought into an argument from physics: the solar and lunar influence exerted on the waters has been so adapted that the tides are raised only to certain heights and cannot overflow the shores or be dissipated into the atmosphere, and in this one economy, he says, there is a whole circle of science — the quantities of matter in sun, moon and earth adjusted to each other, and the laws requiring some of the nicest of the Newtonian calculations to ascertain. C.H. Spurgeon makes the point plainly, that the miracle of the Red Sea is repeated in nature day by day.

The summons that follows is universal. C.H. Spurgeon notes that the psalmist was not blinded by national prejudice and did not restrict the worship to the seed of Abraham; if the far-off nations are not instructed enough to praise, let them at least fear, and what is set down as a wish may be read as a prophecy. Adam Clarke puts the ground of the fear shortly: he who has thus bound can unloose, and he who has created can destroy.
10:
John Wesley marks the transition: the psalm passes from the work of creation to the works of providence, and from God’s power in senseless and irrational creatures to his power in over-ruling the thoughts and wills and actions of men, single or united. John Gill gives the disappointing of wicked counsels its instances — Ahithophel against David, the Egyptians and Assyrians against Israel, Jews and Gentiles against Christ — and observes that however subtly such schemes are contrived they are commonly blasted. Adam Clarke hears the second psalm again, the useless attempts of the nations to prevent the extension of Christ’s kingdom, and applies it to any attempt to stop the promulgation of the Gospel. Charles Ellicott would render the word for devices as thoughts, or better as purposes, in both verses, and finds the point of the passage in the contrast: the counsel of the Lord, being righteous as well as eternal, frustrates the counsel of the heathen while his own people rest in stable peace.

What that standing counsel contains divides them. John Gill excludes the doctrines and ordinances of the Gospel, firm as those are, and makes it the purposes and decrees of God, eternal and unfrustrable, under which fall the choice of persons to everlasting life and their redemption, effectual calling and glorification. Adam Clarke reads it instead as a series of things already done: he determined to make a world and made it, to create man and created him, that at a certain period God should be manifested in the flesh and it was so, that the Gospel should be preached in all the world — and behold, he says, it has already nearly overrun the whole earth. John Wesley compresses it to a line, that all his purposes and designs are always successful. Matthew Henry draws the corollary about human freedom: though God has endued man with understanding and freedom of will, he reserves to himself the government of him, and even of the faculties by which he is qualified to govern himself.

The twelfth verse, which Charles Ellicott calls the pivot on which the whole psalm turns and thinks was sung in full chorus, produces the sharpest division of the chapter over who the blessed nation is. Adam Clarke answers the Jews, elected as his heritage and preserved as such for two thousand years, and then adds that they have been reprobated for their unbelief and rebellion and the Gentiles elected in their place; he also notes that the name here translated God belongs to that economy in which God is manifested in the flesh. John Gill allows the principal regard to be to Israel but refuses the limit, since God is the God of the Gentiles also, and makes the nation the chosen generation and peculiar people drawn from both. C.H. Spurgeon agrees, that Israel was happy in the worship of the only true God while others grovelled before their idols, but that all who confide in the Lord are blessed in the largest sense and none can reverse the blessing; election, he says, is at the bottom of it all, and none take the Lord to be their God till he takes them to be his people.
13:
C.H. Spurgeon takes the repetition as deliberate: the sentiment is worth repeating and needs repeating, since man is most prone to forget it, and as great men sit at their windows watching the crowd below, so the Lord gazes intently on his responsible creatures and forgets nothing of what he sees. All the sons of Adam, he adds, are as well watched as their lone progenitor was in the garden, from the frozen pole to the scorching equator, in huts and palaces alike. John Wesley draws the universal inference: though God has a relation to Israel he has a general care over all mankind, whose hearts and ways he observes. Adam Clarke and John Gill agree in referring the two verses to providence, Gill locating the looking in heaven, where his throne and temple are.

The clause about hearts fashioned alike is read four ways. John Gill takes it of the making: all hearts are alike as they come from God, and the differences that appear afterwards may be owing to the constitution of their bodies, to education, and to their different situations and advantages in life. He allows the rendering together or altogether, not of time as though all were made at once but of equality, and adds that souls are created and not generated. Adam Clarke says the same of the equipment: the same powers, faculties and passions, body and spirit having the same essential properties in every human being. John Wesley shifts the equality from the making to the subjection — having said that God observes all men, the psalmist now adds that he rules them, disposing even the most unmanageable hearts according to the counsel of his will, and all alike fall under his jurisdiction, Jews or Gentiles, princes or peasants. Charles Ellicott redivides the lines to read that God moulds their hearts for all and observes all their deeds, and notes that the verb is the one used of a potter moulding clay.

On the vanity of force Charles Ellicott presses two renderings: that the king does not triumph by the greatness of his force, and that the word given as safety is better read as victory, the allusion being to the war-horse. John Gill keeps safety and observes that a king at the head of a numerous army may still fail to beat a smaller one and be taken by it, so that even such men need saving and cannot save themselves. He explains the horse being called a lie by the idiom — the olive is said to lie when the hope of fruit is disappointed, and the field is called lying in Horace — and takes the horse to stand for every kind of military preparation. John Wesley says the same, that it promises the help and safety it cannot give, and adds that the psalmist instances kings because they are the most uncontrollable persons in the world and the most confident of themselves, which makes them the strongest proof of his general proposition. Adam Clarke answers the horse on its own ground: with all his fleetness he is no sure means of escape, for the lion or the tiger can overtake him, or he may stumble, fall and destroy his rider; and a king is but a man, who may lose his life as easily as one of his common soldiers.
18:
Adam Clarke sets the eighteenth verse against everything before it: though all the above are unavailing, here is one thing that can never fail, the watchful providence of the Most High. John Wesley draws the rule out of it, that whoever would have safety must expect it only from the watchful eye and almighty hand of God, and identifies those who hope as placing their trust and happiness not in any creature but in God alone. John Gill defines the fear as a godly fear, by which men hate evil and are careful not to offend, and adds that the eye upon them is not only of providence, to protect and supply, but of love and grace.

What death they are delivered from divides the two who take it up. John Gill excludes the bodily one: the soul does not die and is never in danger of dying, and those who fear the Lord are not exempted from a corporeal death but die as other men, though they are sometimes remarkably preserved even in a general calamity. He makes it the spiritual death they lay under by nature, from which they are quickened at conversion, and the eternal death that shall never have power over them. Adam Clarke means exactly the bodily one: God watches over them in all sudden dangers and emergencies so that they shall not lose their lives by any accident, and keeps them from a lingering death by extraordinary supplies granted in an extraordinary manner, because he is all in all and everywhere.

The closing verses turn to the first person plural. John Gill assigns them to the church and asks what the waiting is for: either the coming in the flesh and the salvation in it, for which the patriarchs, prophets and all the Old Testament saints waited — the Targum paraphrases it as waiting for the redemption of the Lord — or a spiritual coming and gracious presence after an absence; and since it is the soul that waits, the waiting is hearty, sincere and earnest. Adam Clarke makes it a whole manner of life: our whole life is employed in this blessed work, and we trust in nothing but him, neither in multitudes of armed men nor in natural strength nor in the fleetest animals. C.H. Spurgeon calls waiting a great lesson, and quietness in expectation, patience in hope and singleness in confidence one of the bright attainments of a Christian; he counts the three possessives in the verse and says that personal possession makes the Christian man, all else being mere talk. On the last verse he notes that the mercy is asked in a proportion the Master himself sanctioned, according to their faith, and then asks him to do more than that when hope is faint. John Gill takes the request as a prayer of faith, since the mercy is already upon his people in great plenty, and Adam Clarke as a confession that they cannot abide in this state unless upheld, disclaiming all merit and asking only continuance.
